skyline.text: LLMs predict the next word. So, says Amit Varma, do we.
One root, two journeys and a Chennai street cart
How a twenty-something invented a genre with no precedent

brief.head: Marathon, not sprint
brief.text: The world is hard and complicated, Ajay Shah said, and screaming does not help. He wants calm, curious engagement, sustained like a marathon runner’s energy. {002-C01}

brief.head: AI until it isn’t
brief.text: We call something AI until it becomes commonplace, Amit Varma said. A friend of his noted that, thanks to GPS, young people will never know what getting lost is like. {002-C03}

brief.head: Half man, half engine
brief.text: Chess experts once said a human with an engine would beat either alone. Ajay Shah wants such hybrids for diagnosis. Today, Amit Varma said, that chess claim looks ludicrous. {002-C14}

brief.head: Why be your slave?
brief.text: Amit Varma asked: if an AGI were smarter than us and had an analogue of consciousness, on what basis could we keep it enslaved? {002-C15}

brief.head: Variety as humility
brief.text: Hunter-gatherers ate hundreds of species, Ajay Shah said, and science only found vitamins in the 20th century. A diverse diet respects how little we know about the body. {002-C16}

thought.text: What will remain with you is the joy of creation.
thought.who: Amit Varma, consoling creators who may one day be outsold by machines

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on artificial intelligence
lead.head: Statistics, or the singularity?
body: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah opened their second episode with a song. The show’s name comes from Bruce Springsteen’s *You’re Missing*, from *The Rising*, the album that came out after 9/11.

In it, someone is in an apartment after a loved one has died. The lyrics just list what is there: shirts in the closet, coffee cups on the counter, papers on the doorstep. Then: “Everything is everything, but you’re missing.” {002-S01}

Varma plays it to his writing students: deep emotion needs no fancy adjectives. The phrase also fits the show, he said, because neither host wants to look at the world through one frame. We contain multitudes, and so does the world.
Then they turned to the day’s single subject, artificial intelligence, which Varma said has filled the future with unknown unknowns.
## What’s in a name
Shah began by objecting to the name. Hiding in the phrase AI, he said, is the idea of fluid, creative human intelligence. What exists is statistical models processing data. {002-C02}
Large language models, in his phrase, are “good word prediction engines”, useful and no more.

Varma thought this underrated the machines and overrated us. Creativity seems mystical, he argued, only because we cannot see how our neurons produce it. “I’m saying Beethoven’s brain had nothing but statistical models, and that’s enough to reach that level of creativity.” {002-C04}
Shah’s answer was the Einstein test. Stand in 1905 with every text in the world, he said, and no LLM will produce special relativity. {002-C06}
Varma’s reply was that this is an argument about LLMs, not about AI as a whole.
## Tools for masters

On what the tools are good for, the hosts largely agreed. Shah sees LLMs lifting middling workers to good work, provided a master approves every product. For India, short of masters, he called that “a tool made in heaven”.
His worry is the apprentice. A young coder or writer who leans on the machine, he fears, may never build the craft. Varma replied that the few who truly want mastery will get there anyway.
Both expect machines to take over formulaic work, from romance novels to copywriting. Neither expects lasting unemployment. For creators, Varma said, what remains is the joy of creation.
## Where the wonder is
Shah’s real excitement lay elsewhere. Turn a problem into a game, with fixed rules and a clear reward, and machines discover genuinely new things. {002-C11}

His examples were AlphaZero’s chess, protein folding and the first improvements in 50 years to matrix multiplication. Varma, a keen chess player, described AlphaZero teaching itself the game in a day and then playing like an alien.

Neither host had time for doom. Shah called machine-takeover claims farcical; the real risks, he said, are mundane errors of the kind engineers already trade off. Varma asked why we place the human species on a pedestal at all.
They agreed to disagree, genially, “as AI also would”, Varma said, “because no emotions, we are the messed up creatures”.
Then came the books: a feminist and a monster from Varma, and from Shah, a better masala chai.

second.label: A feminist pioneer
second.head: Why only men, asked Mary
second.deck: Amit Varma on Mary Wollstonecraft, John Locke and the doctors who did not wash
body: Amit Varma’s first recommendation was Mary Wollstonecraft’s *A Vindication of the Rights of Woman*, a classic of feminism he holds close to his heart. {002-R18} Wollstonecraft had read John Locke on natural rights, and asked one question: why should they apply only to men?

The book, Varma said, is as much a work of philosophy as of polemic, and its story is tragic. Wollstonecraft died after childbirth of an infection, because doctors did not yet know they had to wash their hands.
About half a century later, Ignaz Semmelweis did his studies on hand-washing and infection. For some twenty years he was ignored and hounded, Varma said, and he died in a mental asylum. {002-S06}

quote.text: For about twenty years Semmelweis was ignored, he was hounded, he was cancelled because he did not conform to the conventional thinking

photo.hint: portrait of the English writer and philosopher

second.caption: Mary Wollstonecraft

third.head: Nine more murders in Mahim
body: Amit Varma once recorded an eight-hour episode of *The Seen and the Unseen* with the writer Jerry Pinto: perhaps, he said, his most memorable oral history. {002-R08}

Pinto had written a crime thriller, *Murder in Mahim*. Asked if he was writing any more, he said no. Varma predicted that a few years from now you could tell an AI to write nine more books in the series, “and they’ll be so good that Jerry will go, Wow, and he won’t know the difference”. {002-S02}

Ajay Shah turned the same conversation against him. Give a model everything Pinto has written and everything Varma has ever said, he argued, and it still could not produce what passed between them. {#pinto}
“It’s a creative product. It’s a product of that moment,” Shah said.
third.caption: Jerry Pinto’s unwritten sequels

p2.title: Minds and machines
p2.deck: Six rounds of a friendly argument: Ajay Shah on the limits of statistics, Amit Varma against human hubris

sections.label: The first round
sections.head: Clever sums, not a mind
sections.caption: why AI is not AI
body: Ajay Shah would rather not call it AI at all. Hiding in the phrase, he said, is the idea of the fluid general intelligence, creativity and passion of a human being. “Everything that passes for AI in this world are really statistical models that are processing data.” {002-C02}

Shah loves statistics; data analysis is what he has done for a living all his life. A program that flags signs of TB on X-rays is useful, he said. To call it fluid general intelligence would be a farce.
Nor is he pleading for mystery. On the old divide between idealism and materialism, he is a materialist: nothing happens in the skull but the quantum mechanics of its atoms. {002-J11}
## The magic wears off

Amit Varma half agreed. We call things AI only until they become commonplace. Shah’s example was Ken Thompson’s dynamic-programming algorithm for chess endgames, a thunderbolt when it arrived and boring today. {002-J10}
Where Varma parted company was on human hubris. Rubbishing AI at this early stage, he said, is like rubbishing computing in 1950 on seeing a 2MB mainframe that filled a room. {#mainframe}

~ We find art mystical, he argued, only because we don’t know the mechanism. Art and craft are the same thing. Humans run on a fraction of the training data and processing power of modern models, so it seemed to him a no-brainer that machines would eventually do everything we do.

quote.text: We’ll call something AI till it becomes commonplace in part of our lives and then we just treat it as commonplace, as normalized.

sections.label: The second round
sections.head: Every cover drive is elegant
sections.caption: autocomplete on steroids
body: The common jibe is that LLMs are autocorrect on steroids. “Of course they are,” Amit Varma said. “So are we.” {002-C05}

Writers fear cliché above all, he said, citing *The War Against Cliché* by Martin Amis, who had died recently. Cricket talk runs on stock phrases: a cover drive is always elegant, an accurate bowler always has metronomic accuracy.
Even the musician Gaurav Chintamani, he recalled, had asked on *The Seen and the Unseen* whether originality exists at all.
## The next monument
Ajay Shah took a stand for the human race. Something bubbling inside our flesh and blood, he said, makes us wake up and say, “Hey, let me try X.” {#tryx} Only we do that.

Models trained on the past, he argued, stay derivative. Standing at Akbar’s tomb in Sikandra, the state of the art, a model would never come up with the Taj Mahal, the next step in “the great arms race of monuments”. {002-J13}
His use for LLMs is humbler: write the essence of an idea in a terse paragraph and get a thousand-word first draft, which must never be sent off unedited.
~ Varma granted that an LLM might not produce Einstein. But AI, he believed, would be able to come up with Einstein’s discoveries.

quote.text: So I would say that here again, hubris, we might be overestimating ourselves.

sections.label: The third round
sections.head: Q2 in, Q3 out
sections.caption: the tool for a master
body: LLMs are tools, not intelligence, Ajay Shah said, and tools for a master. “The product has to always be approved by a master. The product can never be approved by a junior.” {002-C07}

They are trained on the internet, with all its rubbish, and they hallucinate, inventing completely imaginary facts. His own experiments with text and code went wrong too often to treat the output as final.

Sort workers into quartiles, from Q1, the weakest, to Q4, the masters. Shah’s mental model, borne out by some research, is that an LLM turns a Q2 worker into an approximation of Q3. It is tailor-made for India, he said, which is short of masters, provided management techniques are built around it.
## The apprentice’s problem

His deeper worry was the journey to mastery. {002-C08} Code suggested as you type, he said, kills the problem-solving of the mind; people fixing up ChatGPT’s text may permanently lose the craft of writing. Is it just like the calculator? He thought not.
If he were 17, he said, he would switch off GitHub Copilot and write code from scratch. {#copilot}
~ Amit Varma did not share the fear. In every generation, he said, only a small, self-motivated layer of people seeks mastery. They will get there anyway, and the incentives are now bigger than ever.

quote.text: A good day is one in which you write one good sentence.
quote.who: Hemingway, as quoted by Ajay Shah

sections.label: The fourth round
sections.head: Joy without the applause
sections.caption: thin and thick desire
body: Amit Varma drew a line between two kinds of desire. Thin desire is wanting your work to succeed in the market and win validation. Thick desire is the act of creation, beautiful in and of itself.
At some point, he said, declining to put a date on it, AI will constantly produce great novels, music and operas that no human can compete with. He does not see that as a threat.
What remains is the joy of creation and mastery for its own sake. {002-C09} Those who create for validation, he argued, were doing it for the wrong reason anyway.
## Winner takes all

Ajay Shah, looking even 50 years ahead, expected the tools to kill mass-produced, formulaic work: romance novels churned out by the hundred, screenplays, research papers, opinion pieces. Great works would remain a human preserve, in “a winner takes all world with a vengeance”.
Varma expects copywriting and illustration jobs to vanish. “You don’t need a creative director with ten copywriters. You need a creative director who can prompt.” {002-C10}

~ Neither host feared lasting unemployment. The productivity gains will go back into the economy, Varma said. The market economy of the last 1,000 years absorbed the steam engine and electricity, Shah said, and this is “small change compared to that”. {#upheaval}

quote.text: So the people who are worried about this are worried for the wrong reasons.

sections.label: The fifth round
sections.head: Game on for the machines
sections.caption: machines that discover
body: What excites Ajay Shah is not the chatbot but discovery. When a problem has fixed rules and an objective reward, as chess does, a machine can climb the hill and find new things instead of remixing the past. {002-C11}

AlphaZero, he said, made the hosts think about openings, sacrifice and reward in new ways, and Magnus Carlsen changed his ideas about chess after watching it. Similar methods comprehensively solved questions in protein folding that had long defied human science.
## More engines, more variety

Amit Varma recalled an earlier revolution, around 2003 and 2004, when Stockfish became stronger than the strongest human and players began teaching themselves with computers. Instead of everything becoming homogenised, “it actually went in the opposite direction,” he said. {002-S03}

Engines found concrete exceptions to the Soviet school’s fixed rules about the centre, space and initiative, freeing creative players such as Wesley So and Alireza Firouzja. Anand once noted that in his generation a completely unexpected move was probably a bad one.

~ Shah’s caution was that chess is a finite, closed problem. Most of the world, like a car looking at a scene with imperfect information, is statistical inference under uncertainty, where there can never be a perfect algorithm.

quote.text: The beauty is chess is a finite game with reward function, and you’re able to climb that hill and discover new wonders

sections.label: The last round
sections.head: No paperclip apocalypse
sections.caption: AI alarmism and the real risks
body: Amit Varma laid out the classic nightmare, the paperclip maximizer: an all-powerful machine built to make paperclips goes haywire and turns all organic matter into material for them, until the whole universe is paperclips. {002-R15}
He rejected it twice. If it happened, he asked, why place the human species on a pedestal? {002-C12} And it simply won’t happen, any more than GPS is going to destroy us.
Ajay Shah called machine-takeover claims farcical, science-fiction material. When humans built the automobile, people died in accidents, and we blamed the driver, not the car.
## With probability one

Diagnostic machines will make mistakes and kill people, Shah said, and military robots will kill civilians. “It’s going to happen with probability one.” Every system trades false alarms against misses, and society must weigh the two. {002-C13}

Government need not do all the heavy lifting, Shah said: “I want to be fully Coasean.” {002-J16} His ideal for TB diagnosis is a man-machine hybrid, with a master for the doubtful middle cases. “But the master is expensive,” he said, so firms will be tempted to cut corners.

~ Varma added the seen and the unseen: we see the life lost to an error, not the lives the technology saves. On whether a conscious AGI deserves rights, Shah declined the premise: “I’m just not there.”

quote.text: So all engineering involves finding a design that finds an ethical, legal, and safe trade-off between type one and type two errors.

side.boxText: Amit Varma thinks machine learning could “do the Einsteinian thing”. Ajay Shah disagrees: stand in 1905 with every text in the world in front of you, he said, and no LLM under any prompting scheme will come up with Einstein’s special theory of relativity. {002-C06}

contQuote.text: It’s good. Lots of things are going to happen and we’re going to become more and more effective. We have better machines. That’s all. It’s just a continuation of the machine age.

p3.deck: Chai, chess, code and a monster: the episode’s tales, and what they teach

stories.start: One day I was in Chennai and I was walking around on the street
stories.end: it has many names all over India, then I recommend that you try this
stories.caption: nannari, the root in his chai
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s recommendation, and the long hunt behind it
stories.head: A Chennai root in a Sahyadri cup
body: Years ago, walking down a street in Chennai, Ajay Shah saw a man with a cart selling something he had never seen before, some kind of root. He asked in English what it was. Another customer standing next to him immediately rattled off the plant’s scientific name: Hemidesmus indicus. {#customer}

Shah bought some, wrote the name down and went home to study it. In Tamil it is nannari. It has hints of cardamom and camphor, and in Tamil Nadu it is made into a syrup, often with way too much sugar.

Then, a couple of years ago, Shah was hiking in the Sahyadris near a place called Jivdan. A village woman was making chai, and he asked for ginger. She had none, and offered something else. She brought back a masala chai unlike any he had tasted. {#jivdan}

Shah, who loves masala chai and is always experimenting with recipes, wanted to be sure he never lost it. So he made a voice recording of the woman and her husband saying the root’s Marathi name. {#recording}
The husband dug him a sapling from the hillside: “Take some home for the wife.”

None of Shah’s Marathi-speaking friends had heard the name. Then one day, smelling the root, he made the connection. “I had that aha moment that this smell reminds me of Nannari, the Tamilian root that I had purchased in Chennai,” he said. {002-S08}
~ He triangulated, and it was the same root. Later he found a Tamil Muslim tea recipe that uses it. His advice: grind nannari to a powder and put it in your chai.
stories.why: Local knowledge is scattered across languages and regions. A voice recording, a sapling and a good nose turned two trips, years apart, into one story, and one novel cup of masala chai.
stories.postscript: Amit Varma, no tea drinker, has had Shah’s herbal tea some thirty times. Susan, Shah’s wife, says it isn’t tea: there’s no tea in it. {#susan}

stories.start: 2017 was the next revolution which changed everything.
stories.end: we don't know why it did them. It is a black box over.
stories.caption: AlphaZero’s alien chess
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the engine that taught itself chess
stories.head: Centuries of chess in a day
body: In 2017, Amit Varma said, AlphaZero taught itself chess in twenty-four hours, with no human database, simply by playing against itself. {#selftaught}

Its games followed the same path as humanity’s. It took up the French Defence, fashionable in the 19th century and now known to be suboptimal. It discovered the Berlin Defence, which Kramnik unleashed, Varma said, in 2001. {#berlin} Then it went beyond us, rethinking material against initiative and attacking down the a- and h-files, as Magnus Carlsen later did.
Carlsen’s coach, Peter Heine Nielsen, said: “I always wondered that if aliens with a superior intelligence came to Earth, how would they play chess? And now I know.” {002-S04}
~ Ajay Shah drew his own lesson: there is no need to win back a sacrificed pawn in two or three moves. “It’s okay, take 15 moves.” {#fifteen}

quote.text: It’s an alien intelligence. It is a black box.

stories.start: One was that there is a long-standing problem of matrix multiplication.
stories.end: And then that stronger machine will find an even better sort algorithm.
stories.caption: machines that make better machines
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on machines that improve machines
stories.head: Teaching old algorithms new tricks
body: For about 50 years, Ajay Shah said, the best way to multiply matrices was the Strassen algorithm, and in all that time no human had found a way to do better. {#strassen}

Then scientists turned the problem into a game. They represented the algorithm itself as a parameter vector and optimised it for correctness and speed. The result was the first improvements in 50 years, now going into computer systems all over the world.
DeepMind did the same for sorting code in LLVM, penalising mistakes and slowness, and today we hold better codes for sorting. {002-R12}
~ Readers of science fiction, Shah noted, have long imagined machines that help us make better machines, in a spiral all the way to the singularity. “Well, here we are.” {002-S05}
stories.why: Even computing’s most basic operations had room to improve. The spiral of machines building better machines has begun, Shah said, and it partners with human research: mathematicians now try to prove theorems about what the machines found.
stories.postscript: Amit Varma’s reply: anyone who has seen him wrap bacon round a sausage knows he is “bloody good at protein folding”. {002-J04}

stories.start: And the daughter she gives birth to is Mary Shelley.
stories.end: precedent existing, say, Let me write a novel about a monster, you know?
stories.caption: Frankenstein and its author
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on Mary Wollstonecraft’s daughter
stories.head: The novel no model could write
body: The baby whose birth killed Mary Wollstonecraft grew up, married Percy Shelley and became Mary Shelley. Otherwise, Amit Varma said, she would have been Mary Wollstonecraft II.

In her early twenties, he said, she wrote *Frankenstein*, whose monster has become a metaphor for many modern fears about AI. {002-R19} People call it the first science fiction book; Varma prefers “proto-science fiction”. Its craft can be critiqued with a modern lens, but there was nothing like it before.
Varma tied it back to the episode’s argument. “If you imagine her LLM, there is nothing like that. She’s just creating this new genre, sui generis.” {002-S07}
~ Read the mother’s book and then the daughter’s, he said, and the arc is fascinating. For the whole story he recommended Charlotte Gordon’s *Romantic Outlaws*. {002-R20}
stories.why: A model trained only on what came before, Varma suggested, would not have written *Frankenstein*. From the mother’s “Why not women also?” to the daughter’s monster, two lives show what genuinely new creation looks like.

quiz.q: Which Bruce Springsteen song gave the show its name, and what is it about?
quiz.a: *You’re Missing*, about an apartment after a loved one died in 9/11.

quiz.q: Which theory, Ajay Shah argued, could no LLM with every text of 1905 invent?
quiz.a: Einstein’s special theory of relativity: a corpus without it cannot produce it.

quiz.q: In Ajay Shah’s quartile model, what can an LLM do for a Q2 worker?
quiz.a: Lift them to roughly Q3 work, as long as a master approves it.

quiz.q: What did Carlsen’s coach Peter Heine Nielsen say AlphaZero had finally shown him?
quiz.a: How aliens with a superior intelligence would play chess if they came to Earth.

quiz.q: Why, according to Amit Varma, did Mary Wollstonecraft die after giving birth?
quiz.a: An infection: doctors did not yet know they had to wash their hands.

quiz.q: Where did Ajay Shah first meet nannari, and where did he taste it in chai?
quiz.a: From a cart on a Chennai street; in a village near Jivdan.
